{{Short description|Algebraic curve}}
[[File:Kartesisches-Blatt.svg|thumb|250px|right|The folium of Descartes (green) with asymptote (blue), when <math display="inline">a=1</math>]]
In [[geometry]], the '''folium of Descartes''' ({{ety|la|folium|[[leaf]]}}) is an [[algebraic curve]] defined by the [[implicit equation]] <math>x^3 + y^3 - 3ayx = 0 </math>. It is named after the mathematician and philosopher [[René Descartes]].

== History ==
The curve was first proposed and studied in 1638 by René Descartes,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=June 5, 2020|title=Folium of Descartes|url=https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Folium_of_Descartes|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=January 30, 2021|website=Encyclopedia of Mathematics}}</ref> who was interested in classifying curves by the [[Degree of a polynomial|degrees]] of their algebraic equations.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Kline |first=Morris |author-link=Morris Kline |title=Mathematical Thought from Ancient to Modern Times |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1972 |isbn=0-19-506136-5 |pages= |chapter=}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=314}} Its claim to fame lies in an incident in the development of [[calculus]]. Descartes challenged [[Pierre de Fermat]] to find the [[tangent]] line to the curve at an arbitrary point, since Fermat had recently discovered a method for finding tangent lines. Fermat solved the problem easily, something Descartes was unable to do.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Simmons |first=George |author-link=George F. Simmons |title=Calculus Gems: Brief Lives and Memorable Mathematics |publisher=McGraw-Hill |year=1992 |isbn=978-0-070-57566-0 |location=New York}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=101}} Since the invention of calculus, the slope of the tangent line can be found easily using [[implicit differentiation]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Stewart |first=James |author-link=James Stewart (mathematician) |title=Calculus: Early Transcendentals |publisher=Cengage Learning |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-538-49790-9 |edition=7th |location= |pages= |chapter=}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=209–11}}

== Graphing the curve ==
{{Descartes|expanded=Mathematics}}

The folium of Descartes can be expressed in [[polar coordinates]] as<math display="block">r = \frac{3 a \sin \theta \cos \theta}{\sin^3 \theta + \cos^3 \theta },</math>which is plotted on the left. This is equivalent to<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|page=687}}

<math>r = \frac{3a \sec\theta \tan\theta}{1 + \tan^3 \theta}.</math>

Another technique is to write <math>y = px</math> and solve for <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> in terms of <math>p</math>. This yields the [[Rational function|rational]] [[parametric equations]]:<ref>{{cite web |last=Wildberger |first=N.J. |date=4 August 2013 |title=DiffGeom3: Parametrized curves and algebraic curves |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jG4DYZ5uuE0 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/jG4DYZ5uuE0 |archive-date=2021-12-21 |accessdate=5 September 2013 |website=www.youtube.com |publisher=[[University of New South Wales]]}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

: <math>x = {{3ap} \over {1 + p^3}},\, y = {{3ap^2} \over {1 + p^3}}. </math>

We can see that the parameter is related to the position on the curve as follows:
* <math>p < -1</math> corresponds to <math>x>0</math>, <math>y<0</math>: the right, lower, "wing".
* <math>-1 < p < 0</math> corresponds to <math>x<0</math>, <math>y>0</math>: the left, upper "wing".
* <math>p>0</math> corresponds to <math>x>0</math>, <math>y>0</math>: the loop of the curve.

Another way of plotting the function can be derived from symmetry over <math>y = x</math>. The symmetry can be seen directly from its equation (x and y can be interchanged). By applying rotation of 45° clockwise for example, one can plot the function symmetric over rotated x axis.[[File:Декартов лист в полярных координатах.png|left|thumb|304x304px|Folium of Descartes in polar coordinates ''r-φ:'' <math display="inline">r(\phi)/a,\,a=1 </math>]]This operation is equivalent to a substitution:<math display="block"> x = {{u+v} \over {\sqrt{2}}},\, y = {{u-v} \over {\sqrt{2}}} </math>and yields<math display="block"> v=\pm u\sqrt{\frac{3a\sqrt{2}-2u}{6u+3a\sqrt{2}}}\,,\,u<3a/\sqrt{2}. </math>Plotting in the Cartesian system of <math>(u,v)</math> gives the ''folium'' rotated by 45° and therefore symmetric by <math>u</math>-axis.

== Properties ==
It forms a loop in the first quadrant with a [[Singular point of a curve|double point]] at the origin and has [[asymptote]]<math display="block">x+y=-a \,.</math>It is symmetrical about the line <math>y = x</math>. As such, the curve and this line intersect at the origin and at the point <math display="inline">(3a/2,3a/2).</math>

Implicit differentiation gives the formula for the slope of the tangent line to this curve to be<ref name=":1" />

:<math>\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{ay-x^2}{y^2-ax}\,, </math> 

with poles <math display="inline">x=y^2/a</math> and value 0 or <math>\pm \infty</math> at the origin.

Using either one of the polar representations above, the area of the interior of the loop is found to be <math display="inline"> 3a^2 / 2</math>. Moreover, the area between the "wings" of the curve and its slanted asymptote is also <math display="inline">3a^2/2.</math><ref name=":0" />

== Relationship to the trisectrix of Maclaurin ==
[[File:MaclaurinTrisectrix.SVG|thumb|Trisectrix of Maclaurin]]
The folium of Descartes is related to the [[trisectrix of Maclaurin]] by [[affine transformation]]. To see this, start with the equation<math display="block">x^3+y^3=3a\cdot xy\,,</math>and change variables to find the equation in a coordinate system rotated 45 degrees. This amounts to setting  

<math display="block">x = {{X+Y} \over \sqrt{2}}, y = {{X-Y} \over \sqrt{2}}.</math>In the <math>X,Y</math> plane the equation is<math display="block">2X(X^2 + 3Y^2) = 3 \sqrt{2}a(X^2-Y^2).</math>

If we stretch the curve in the <math>Y</math> direction by a factor of <math>\sqrt{3}</math> this becomes<math display="block">2X(X^2 + Y^2) = a \sqrt{2}(3X^2-Y^2),</math>which is the equation of the trisectrix of Maclaurin.
